title: USP13 facilitates a ferroptosis-to-autophagy switch by activation of the NFE2L2/NRF2-SQSTM1/p62-KEAP1 axis dependent on the KRAS signaling pathway
author: Ling Chen; Jieling Ning; Li Linghu; Jun Tang; Na Liu; Yao Long; Jingyue Sun; Cairui Lv; Ying Shi; Tania Tao; Desheng Xiao; Ya Cao; Xiang Wang; Shuang Liu; Guangjian Li; Bin Zhang; Yongguang Tao
text:
ABSTRACT
Macroautophagy/autophagyis a lysosomal-regulated degradation process that participates incellular stress and then promotes cell survival or triggers celldeath. Ferroptosis was initially described as anautophagy-independent, iron-regulated, nonapoptotic cell death.However, recent studies have revealed that autophagy is positivelyassociated with sensitivity to ferroptosis. Nonetheless, themolecular mechanisms by which these two types of regulated cell death(RCD) modulate each other remain largely unclear. Here, we screened85 deubiquitinating enzymes (DUBs) and found that overexpression ofUSP13 (ubiquitin specific peptidase 13) could significantlyupregulate NFE2L2/NRF2 (NFE2 like bZIP transcription factor 2)protein levels. In addition, in 39 cases of KRAS-mutated lungadenocarcinoma (LUAD), we found that approximately 76% of USP13overexpression is positively correlated with NFE2L2 overexpression.USP13 interacts with and catalyzes the deubiquitination of thetranscription factor NFE2L2. Additionally, USP13 depletion promotesan autophagy-to-ferroptosis switch invitro andin xenograft tumor mouse models, through the activation of theNFE2L2-SQSTM1/p62 (sequestosome 1)-KEAP1 axis in KRAS mutant cellsand tumor tissues. Hence, targeting USP13 effectively switchedautophagy-to-ferroptosis, thereby inhibiting KRAS (KRASproto-oncogene, GTPase) mutant LUAD, suggesting the therapeuticpromise of combining autophagy and ferroptosis in the KRAS-mutantLUAD.

KEYWORDS: Autophagy, ferroptosis, LUAD, NFE2L2, SQSTM1, USP13
Introduction
Autophagy is a conserved mechanism in eukaryotes, characterized by the formation of lipid-associated membrane structures (phagophores [PGs], autophagosomes [APs], and autolysosomes [ALs]) that engulf and degrade different cargos (such as excess proteins, invading pathogens, or damaged organelles), which are involved in maintaining cellular homeostasis when cells confront with nutritional deficits [1–4].
Autophagy degrades various cellular components. Autophagy can be nonselective and is associated with the indiscriminate sequestration and degradation of cytoplasmic components. Conversely, selective autophagy degrades specific targets, such as damaged organelle, aggregated proteins, or invading bacteria, thus being crucial in cellular quality control [4]. Autophagy dysfunction has been linked to several diseases, including infections, neurodegenerative diseases, inflammation, metabolic disorders, cancer and aging [5]. Autophagy is a major degradation pathway that promotes the anabolism of cancer cells and depends on MTOR (mechanistic target or rapamycin kinase) and the ATG (autophagy related) protein family working in a coordinated fashion [6,7]. Autophagy mediates lipid metabolism, lipid droplet storage, and dysfunction of this axis is associated with metabolic disorders [6,8]. Lipid metabolism is closely associated with another type of regulated cell death (RCD), named ferroptosis, a form of cell death caused by excessive lipid peroxidation and the accumulation of free unstable iron [8,9]. Ferroptosis is associated with notable morphological changes in mitochondria, which become smaller than normal mitochondria with condensed membrane densities and reduction or vanishing of the crista [10,11]. Oxidative stress and the lipid peroxidation products, malondialdehyde (MDA) and 4-hydroxynonenal (4HNE) are involved in inducing autophagosomes formation [12,13]. TMEM164 (transmembrane protein 164) selectively mediates ATG5-dependent autophagosome formation during ferroptosis and degrades ferritin, GPX4, and lipid droplets, thereby increasing iron accumulation and lipid peroxidation, and promoting ferroptosis [14]. However, the molecular mechanisms underlying the interplay between autophagy and ferroptosis remain unelucidated.
Many cancer cells are addicted to autophagy to combat high levels of proteotoxic, metabolism, oxidative and hypoxia conditions [15]. Cancers driven by KRAS mutation especially are dependent heavily on autophagy for their growth and invasion [15–17]. KRAS mutations occur very frequently in pancreatic (>90–5%), colorectal (40%), and lung cancers (20%). An important characteristic of oncogenic KRAS expression is the early upregulation of cellular reactive oxygen species (ROS), which promotes cellular transformation to escape cell death [18]. The KRAS and MYC oncogene products constitutively increase NFE2L2 transcription, thereby enhancing the basic activity of antioxidants and promoting cellular detoxification programs, through the RAF-MAP2K/MEK-MAPK/ERK (mitogen-activated protein kinase)-JUN pathway [19,20]. Clinical development of RAS therapies has found encouraging signals of efficacy in the treatment of highly refractory malignancies [21].
NFE2L2 is a major transcriptional regulator of redox homeostasis [22–26], and is regulated by the ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS). Under basic conditions, NFE2L2 protein levels are low because of the regulation of KEAP1, a substrate adaptor of the CUL3 (cullin3)-based E3 ubiquitin ligase that targets to NFE2L2 proteasome degradation [27–29]. When cells are exposed to oxidative stress, KEAP1 is inactivated, leading to stable NFE2L2 nuclear translocation, and activation of cell protection and antioxidant response genes, such as SQSTM1, SLC7A11/xCT (a cystine/glutamate exchange transporter), and NQO1 (NAD(P)H quinone dehydrogenase 1) [30–34]. SQSTM1 is a cytosolic protein containing a ubiquitin-binding domain and an LC3-interacting region/LIR (binding to Atg8-family proteins on the autophagic membrane). In selective autophagy, SQSTM1 binds to ubiquitinated proteins through its UBA domain and interacts with LC3 on autophagosomes through its LC3-interacting region domain, which is responsible for the recruitment of the autophagic membrane to form autophagosomes, and mediates the autophagic clearance [35,36]. Furthermore, SQSTM1 interferes with the interaction between NFE2L2-KEAP1 or promotes the sequestration of KEAP1 and its autophagic degradation [31,32], which then acts as a positive feedback regulator of NFE2L2 and stabilizes it [37]. After oxidative stress, the expression level of cystine/glutamate exchange transporter SLC7A11 mediated by NFE2L2 is increased, which promotes the uptake of cystine and its reduction to cysteine to suppress ferroptosis [38,39].
USP13 is a crucial member of the USP subfamily which regulates the ubiquitination status of diverse substrates involved in multiple processes, including cell cycle, autophagy, metabolism, innate antiviral immunity, and DNA repair response [9,40–43]. In the present study, we found that USP13 was overexpressed in approximately 76% of LUAD cases KRAS mutations, which, along with NFE2L2 overexpressed, and USP13 might positively upregulate the NFE2L2 protein level by stabilizing it. Additionally, USP13 facilitated the ferroptosis to autophagy switch through the activation of the NFE2L2-SQSTM1-KEAP1 axis in KRAS mutant cells and tumor tissues. We also demonstrate that targeting USP13 enhanced autophagy to the ferroptosis switch and promoted KRAS mutant LUAD suppression both in vitro and in vivo. USP13 plays an important role in NFE2L2 turnover by protecting cells from oxidative stress.
Results
USP13 is a novel DUB of NFE2L2 and deubiquitinates NFE2L2 at K63
NFE2L2 is tightly controlled by the ubiquitin-proteasome system [44,45]. The E3 ligases of NFE2L2 have been elucidated, however, the DUBs that regulate NFE2L2 remain largely unexplored. To identify the DUBs that regulate NFE2L2, we transfected 85 DUB plasmids with the Flag fusion protein into HEK293T cells, and western blot analysis showed that NFE2L2 was significantly upregulated by USP13 overexpression (Figure 1A, Fig. S1A – F). Subsequently, we selected seven DUB plasmids (USP13, USP25, OTUB1, OTUD4, OTUD5, OTUD6B and OTUD7B) that upregulated NFE2L2 expression in 293T cells then transfected into H1299 cells. Western blot analysis revealed that USP13 significantly enhanced NFE2L2 expression (Figure 1B). To further explore the correlation between USP13 and NFE2L2, a significant correlation was found between the expression levels of USP13 and NFE2L2 (p = 8.3e-14, R = 0.24) through the prediction of the protein interaction website GEPIA (http://gepia.cancer-pku.cn/) (Figure 1C). Further, we detected the protein expression levels of USP13 and NFE2L2 in 58 pairs of lung cancer and adjacent tissues, among them, 39 pairs were of LUAD with KRAS mutations, 13 pairs of LUAD with KRAS wildtype, and 6 pairs of lung squamous cell carcinoma (LCSC). We found that the expression levels of both USP13 and NFE2L2 increased in 30 pairs of LUAD with KRAS mutation (Fig. S2A), and no obvious correlation was present between the expression of USP13 and NFE2L2 in 13 pairs of KRAS wild-type LUAD and six pairs of LCSC (Fig. S2B and C). We further quantified and correlated the expression of USP13 and NFE2L2 proteins in 39 pairs of LUAD tissues with KRAS mutation, and the results showed that there was a significant correlation between those two groups in LUAD with KRAS mutation (Figure 1D). In addition, the number of normal bronchial epithelial cells (HBE) and LUAD cells (H1299, H358, A549, and H23) was determined. The results further confirmed that NFE2L2 and USP13 protein levels were positive correlation in two KRAS mutant types of cell lines (H23 and A549), however, no positive correlation in H1299 (Hras mutant), H358 (KRAS mutant, though without KEAP1 mutated) cells [25,46], and HBE cells which had no mutations in KEAP1, NFE2L2, TP53, or KRAS and have basal levels of p-MAPK/ERK [46,47] (Figure 1E), indicating that the correlation between the positive expression of USP13 and NFE2L2 is related to the mutation of KRAS.
Furthermore, we used two different effective sgRNAs to knock down USP13 in A549 cells. Two other stable overexpressed wild-type USP13 or its catalytic mutant with Cys345 mutattion to Ala (USP13C345A) A549 cells were constructed. The expression of UPS13-sgRNAs significantly reduced the expression of NFE2L2 and its downstream genes. Overexpression of wild type USP13, but not USP13C345A, upregulated NFE2L2 and its downstream gene protein levels, SQSTM1, SLC7A11, and NOQ1 (Figure 1F,G). As USP13 is a deubiquitinating enzyme, we determined whether USP13 increases NFE2L2 expression through its deubiquitinating enzyme activity. As expected, NFE2L2 mRNA levels did not change with the reduction in USP13 expression (Fig. S2D). The decreased protein level of NFE2L2 caused by USP13 depletion and the increase in the protein level of NFE2L2 caused by USP13 overexpression, but not USP13C345A, were rescued by treatment with the ubiquitin proteasome inhibitor, MG132 (Figure 1H,I). However, the decreased protein level of NFE2L2 by reduction of USP13 was not rescued after being treated with lysosome autophagy inhibitor Lys01 trihydrochloride (Lys05) (Fig. S2E and F). In addition, when USP13 was overexpressed in A549 cells, the half-life of NFE2L2 was markedly increased (Fig. S2G). These results suggest that USP13 might affects the protein stability of NFE2L2 through the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway.
Next, we investigated whether USP13 cleaved the polyubiquitin chains of NFE2L2. We found that USP13 rather than the enzymatically inactive mutant USP13C345A catalyzed NFE2L2 deubiquitination (Figure 1J), suggesting that USP13 increases the stability of NFE2L2 through the ubiquitin proteasome pathway. To determine whether NFE2L2 was a direct substrate of USP13, we then purified USP13, USP13C345A, and ubiquitinated NFE2L2 from 293T cells, and incubated them in a cell-free system. Wild-type USP13, but not its catalytically inactive mutant USP13C345A, decreased NRF poly-ubiquitination by 70–80% in vitro (Figure 1K), indicating that USP13 might directly deubiquitinate NFE2L2. We then transfected NFE2L2 along with ubiquitin wild-type, or a single lysine residue (KO) ubiquitin mutant in the presence or absence of USP13, and then performed deubiquitination analysis. The results showed that USP13 catalyzed the removal of K63 linked polyubiquitin chains from NFE2L2 (Figure 1L). Next, we transfected MYC-USP13 and Flag-NFE2L2 constructs into 293T cells for a co-immunoprecipitation (Co-IP) assay to confirm the interaction between USP13 and NFE2L2. IP with an anti-MYC antibody demonstrated that MYC-USP13 interacted with over-expressed Flag-NFE2L2. Finally, reciprocal IP using an anti-Flag antibody confirmed this interaction (Figure 1M), indicating that USP13 deubiquitinates NFE2L2 by binding to NFE2L2. To identify whether an interaction also occurred between endogenous USP13 and NFE2L2 in lung cancer cells, IP with each antibody detected both USP13 and NFE2L2, suggesting that the endogenous proteins interacted in A549 cells (Figure 1N). Then, we mapped the domains that mediated NFE2L2-USP13 association and found that amino acids (aa) 301–624 domain of USP13 was responsible for their association (Figure 1O,P), suggesting that the structural domain of USP13 (aa 301–624) but not the C terminus, the UBP domain or the N terminus domain, was the primary determinant for their association with NFE2L2.
Collectively, these results suggested that USP13 stabilized NFE2L2 by interacting with and deubiquitinating its protein and mainly catalyzes the removal of K63 linked polyubiquitin chains from NFE2L2.
USP13 facilitates autophagy via the NFE2L2-SQSTM1-KEAP1 axis
As SQSTM1 actively regulates NFE2L2 by interfering with the NFE2L2-KEAP1 interaction or promoting KEAP isolation and autophagic degradation [32]. After dissociating from KEAP1, NFE2L2 stabilizes and subsequently translocates into the nucleus to activate its target genes [48]. We investigated whether USP13 activates NFE2L2 through the NFE2L2-SQSTM1-KEAP1 axis. Therefore, mRNA and protein levels of NFE2L2, SQSTM1 and KEAP1 were measured. Compared to control cells, no obvious change in the mRNA levels of Keap1 and NFE2L2 was noticed in USP13 knock down cells, whereas SQSTM1 mRNA expression was significant reduced (Figure 2A). USP13 overexpression increased NFE2L2 and SQSTM1 protein levels and decreased KEAP1 (Fig. S3A and B). Moreover, overexpression of wild-type USP13, though not its catalytically inactive mutant USP13C345A, increased NFE2L2 and SQSTM1 and decreased KEAP1 protein levels (Figure 2B,C), whereas reduction of USP13 significantly decreased the NFE2L2 and SQSTM1, and increased KEAP1 protein levels (Figure 2D). We also performed cycloheximide chase experiments to elucidate the role of USP13 in stabilizing NFE2L2, SQSTM1 and KEAP1 proteins. Both USP13 overexpression and depletion experiments showed that USP13 stabilized NFE2L2 and SQSTM1, however, destabilized the KEAP1 (Figure 2E–H). Collectively, these results indicate that USP13 modulats NFE2L2 and KEAP1 at their protein level and regulates SQSTM1 at both the protein and mRNA levels.
Next, we sought to explain the USP13-mediated stability of SQSTM1 and KEAP1. We adjusted the protein expression level in the cell lysate to be consistent, and then performed IP assays. As aforementioned, KEAP1 is a negative regulator of NFE2L2 stability and USP13 displaced KEAP1 from NFE2L2 (Figure 2I,J). SQSTM1 also increases NFE2L2 stablity, for USP13 was observed to enhance the SQSTM1-NFE2L2 (Figure 2K) or KEAP1-SQSTM1 interaction (Figure 2L). Simultaneously, we overexpressed USP13 in A549 cells and did a concentration gradient of USP13. The IP results showed that KEAP1 bound to SQSTM1 decreased with an increase in SQSTM1 expression (Fig. S3C), which suggested that USP13 promoted the binding of SQSTM1 to KEAP1, and that SQSTM1 sequestered KEAP1 for its autophagic degradation. Thus, USP13 May increase the transcription of SQSTM1 by upregulating the protein stability of NFE2L2 to improve the protein stability of SQSTM1 and reduce the protein stability of KEAP1.
USP13 facilitates autophagy [43], and LC3B is a marker of autophagosomes and lipidation of the LC3 protein (the conversion of LC3B-I to LC3B-II), which has frequently been employed as a marker of autophagosome formation [49]. We constructed NFE2L2 knockout (KO) A549 cells by using CRISPR-Cas9 technology. Subsequently, we overexpressed Vector, wild-type, and mutant plasmids of USP13 in NFE2L2 WT and KO A549 cells. The results showed that the overexpressed USP13 in NFE2L2 WT A549 cells increased the protein levels of SQSTM1 and lipidation of the LC3, however, did not affect them in NFE2L2 KO A549 cells (Figure 2M). The regulation of SQSTM1 and LC3B by USP13 was suggested to depend on NFE2L2. As SQSTM1 acted as a scaffold for protein aggregates formation, and it served as an autophagy receptor, connecting ubiquitin-labeled protein aggregates and recruiting LC3B for autophagy-mediated degradation [49,50], we detected the ubiquitination level of SQSTM1 and LC3B. We knocked down USP13 expression in NFE2L2 WT and KO A549 cells. In the absence of NFE2L2, the ubiquitination level of SQSTM1 did not change due to the depletion of USP13. However, in the presence of NFE2L2, the ubiquitination level of SQSTM1 decreased due to a decrease in USP13 protein levels. Similarly, in the absence of NFE2L2 protein expression, USP13 knockdown did not affect the SQSTM1, Ub-SQSTM1, or LC3 protein levels (Figure 2N).
To test whether USP13 is a negative or positive regulator of autophagy, we observed that basal and chloroquine (CQ, an autophagy inhibitor that prevents lysosomal protein degradation)-reduced autophagy flux was attenuated in USP13 depleted cells compared to the control cells (Figure 2O). Conversely, rescued USP13 increased the LC3B levels in A549 cells (Figure 2P). These data show that USP13 is a positive regulator of autophagy; thus, the reduction in Ub, SQSTM1 and LC3B in USP13-depleted cells was not due to enhanced autophagic flux. Moreover, rescued SQSTM1 could positively affected the protein expression of NFE2L2 and increased the lipidation of the LC3 protein, however, reduced KEAP1 (Figure 2P). Collectively, USP13 activated SQSTM1-LC3 pathway dependent autophagy relies on NFE2L2, and SQSTM1 increases NFE2L2 stability via the autophagic degradation of KEAP1. These results indicated that USP13-facilitated autophagy dependent on stabilizing NFE2L2 via the NFE2L2-SQSTM1-kEAP1 axis.
KRAS status is a crucial factor for the regulation of USP13 to the stabilization and nuclear localization of NFE2L2
As shown in Figure 1, the regulation of NFE2L2 protein stability by USP13 depends on KRAS status. Therefore, we examined the expression of NFE2L2 in the cytoplasm and nucleus of KRAS-mutant (A549 and H460) and wild-type (H1299 and HBE) cells. Compared to that in the control cells, NFE2L2 nuclear levels were substantially more in USP13 overexpressed-A549 and H460 cells (Fig. S4A – D), whereas overexpression of USP13 did not increase the NFE2L2 nuclear levels in H1299 cells (Fig. S4E and F). Moreover, overexpression of wild-type USP13, though not its catalytically inactive mutant USP13C345A, significantly increased NFE2L2 nuclear levels in A549 and H460 cells, however, not in H1299 and HBE cells (Figure 3A–H). Through immunofluorescence (IF) experiments, we observed the colocalization of USP13 and NFE2L2, which further verified their interaction. By merging DAPI (used to stain the nucleus) and NFE2L2, USP13 was observed to promote the translocation of NFE2L2 to the nucleus of A549 cells significantly more than that of H1299 cells (Figure 3I–K). Collectively, these data together suggested that USP13 brought about the stabilization, nuclear translocation, and activation of NFE2L2 dependent on the KRAS mutant status.
Depletion of USP13 switches autophagy to ferroptosis
USP13 upregulates the NFE2L2-SQSTM1-KEAP1 axis, promoting lipidation of LC3B (Figure 2M–P), and increasing SLC7A11 protein levels (Figure 1F,G), which are key molecules that regulated autophagy or ferroptosis [4,39]. Therefore, we performed gene set enrichment analysis/GSEA for the USP13 based on Gene Ontology and WP_FERROPTOSIS sets to explore whether USP13 could regulate ferroptosis in addition to autophagy and apoptosis [43,51]. USP13 expression was associated with ferroptosis (Figure 4A). To validate our bioinformatics results, we treated USP13 knockdown A549 cells with the ferroptosis inducer erastin, the autophagy inducer rapamycin (RAPA), the apoptosis inducer doxorubicin (DOX), and their related cell death inhibitors (ferrostatin-1 [Ferr-1], CQ, and Z-VAD-FMK). Using light microscopy and trypan blue to count the number of dead cells, we found that USP13 depletion significantly promoted ferroptosis, though not autophagy and apoptosis, compared to the sgCtrl group. Furthermore, knockdown of USP13 induced ferroptosis was rescued by Ferr-1 completely (Figure 4B,C). The Cell Counting Kit-8 (CCK8) assay was used to detect the cell viability. Erastin and RAPA treatment promoted cell death, while ferroptosis or autophagy inhibitors (Ferr-1 and CQ) rescued sgUSP13- or sgCtrl-induced cell death (Figure 4D). As autophagy might not be obvious under the microscope and in sufficient glucose medium (Figure 4B,C) [40], western blot of LC3 further confirmed that autophagy was inhibited in the depletion of USP13, compared to that in the sgCtrl group, especially in RAPA-treated cells. Moreover, the ferroptosis marker SLC7A11 but not ACSL4, decreased when USP13 was depleted, regardless of RAPA treatment (Figure 4E). We also observed a significant increase in LC3B puncta formation in the presence of USP13 compared to that in the sgUSP13 groups, whereas a significant decrease in LC3B spot formation was observed when USP13 was knocked down, especially in cells treated with RAPA (Fig. S5A, B). Next, we performed western blot to detect markers of mitochondrial oxidative stress-induced apoptosis as well [52,53], USP13 could affect the protein expression level of BCL2L1/BCL-xL (BCL2 like 1) though not that of BAX (Fig. S5C), which was consistent with a previous report [54]. In addition, when NFE2L2 was knocked out, BAX expression increased regardless of the absence of USP13 (Fig. S5C). These results suggested that the regulation of BCL2L1 by USP13 and the effect of NFE2L2 on BAX are unrelated to the USP13-NFE2L2 pathway, indicating that the USP13-NFE2L2 pathway is more closely related to ferroptosis and autophagy. Autophagy and ferroptosis were observed using transmission electron microscopy (TEM). The results showed that USP13 knockdown decreased ALs and increased shrunken mitochondria compared to those in the Ctrl group (Figure 4F–H). According to the IF assay, compared to sgCtrl cells, LC3B puncta formation was significantly decreased especially cells treated with RAPA in USP13 depletion cells, whereas lipid ROS were obviously increased regardless of RAPA treatment in USP13 depletion cells (Figure 4I–K). These results suggested that USP13 promotes autophagy and inhibits ferroptosis, and that RAPA treatment has no significant effect on ferroptosis.
To investigate whether SQSTM1 promotes or inhibits autophagic flux, we treated cells with CQ. As a classic substrate of autophagy degradation, the switch from LC3-I to LC3-II changed consistently along with SQSTM1 expression under DMSO or CQ treatment conditions (Fig. S5D). Conversely, SQSTM1 rescue increased LC3B levels in A549 cells (Figure 2P). These results demonstrated that SQSTM1 expression promotes autophagy flux, which is dependent on LC3 expression. Additionally, we performed knockdown experiments for SQSTM1 or KEAP1 in both the absence and presence of USP13 to investigate NFE2L2 levels, as well as to assess autophagy responses and autophagy-related ferroptotic targets, such as, GPX4 (glutathione peroxidase 4) and ferritin [14] (Fig. S5E and F). In the case of both SQSTM1 and USP13 knockdown, there was much more decrease in NFE2L2 and SQSTM1 protein levels than only SQSTM1 knockdown, for USP13-decreased NFE2L2 also reduced SQSTM1. Depleted SQSTM1 could also positively affect NFE2L2; therefore, the NFE2L2 protein level in the SQSTM1 knockdown group was lower than that in the control group (Fig, S5E). In the case of both KEAP1 and USP13 knockdown, the reduction in USP13 protein levels decreased the level of NFE2L2, and SQSTM1 protein, which lead to an increase in KEAP1. KEAP1 depletion reduced NFE2L2 binding to KEAP1, therefore, NFE2L2 protein levels in the KEAP1 knockdown group were higher than those in the control group regardless of USP13 depletion. These results further indicated that SQSTM1 and KEAP1 are involved in the regulation of NFE2L2 protein stability by USP13. Due to the decrease in USP13, the protein level of ferritin increased, because the decrease in USP13 reduced the degradation of ferritin by autophagy; the GPX4 protein significantly decreased, which might be due to the reduction of SLC7A11, leading to a decrease in GPX4 synthesis [55], which was greater than the effect of autophagy on the decrease in GPX4 degradation. The final expression of GPX4 decreased at the protein level, which was different from the increase observed in the research [14]. We speculated that this was because the background of the tumors was different and the KRAS pathway was activated in our system.
These results suggested that USP13 mostly regulates autophagy and ferroptosis in A549 cells, and that there may be an antagonistic relationship between autophagy and ferroptosis, for USP13 probably inhibits ferroptosis via the NFE2L2-SLC7A11-GPX4 axis and facilitates autophagy via the NFE2L2-SQSTM1-LC3 axis.
Depletion of USP13 switches autophagy to ferroptosis dependent on the activation of KRAS signaling pathway
The results in Figures 3 and 4 suggested that USP13 might both regulate ferroptosis and autophagy through USP13-promoted NFE2L2 stability, which is dependent on the status of KRAS. Therefore, we explored whether the KRAS affected USP13 regulated ferroptosis and autophagy. Compared with that of the control cells, western blot results showed that the conversion of LC3B-I to LC3B-II in USP13 knockdown H1299 cells did not change with or without RAPA treatment. Moreover, the SLC7A11 and ACSL4 protein levels did not change (Figure 5A). LC3B puncta formation was inhibited in USP13 depleted-A549 cells, though not in USP13 depleted-H1299 cells compared to their control groups after RAPA treatment. In addition, USP13 and LC3B were co-localized in A549 cells (Fig. S5A and B, S6A – D). These results also suggested that USP13 interacts with LC3B by binding to the NFE2L2-SQSTM1-KEAP1 complex [56]. Similarly, the knockdown of USP13 in H1299 cells had negligible effect on LC3B puncta and lipid ROS formation, with or without RAPA treatment (Figure 5B–D). The accumulation of LC3B puncta suggests either autophagic activation or inhibition of downstream autophagic steps. CQ blocks autophagic flux by reducing autophagosome-lysosome fusion [57]. Therefore, the conversion of LC3B-I to LC3B-II decreased, and SLC7A11, though not ACSL4 (acyl-CoA synthetase long-chain family member 4), was reduced in USP13 depleted-A549 cells rather than in USP13 depleted-H1299 compared to that in the sgCtrl groups. Moreover, after CQ treatment, the conversion of LC3B-I to LC3B-II increased, which did not rescue the effect of USP13 knockdown on the reduction of the lipidation of LC3B in A549 cells (Fig. S6E and F). Thus, the accumulation of LC3B puncta here suggested the autophagic activation similar to Figure 2O and S5D.
Treatment with the autophagy inducer RAPA did not significantly affect the regulation of ferroptosis by USP13 (Figure 4E,I). Therefore, we treated cells with the ferroptosis inducer imidazole ketone erastin (IKE) to explore its effect on ferroptosis and autophagy regulated by USP13, and to explore whether it is related to the status of KRAS. In KRAS mutated cell lines A549 and H460, IKE induction slightly upregulates USP13, leading to the upregulation of NFE2L2 and its downstream target genes SQSTM1 and SLC7A11, thus increasing autophagy for the conversion of LC3B-I to LC3B-II enhanced, KEAP1 decreased, and inhibition of ferroptosis, for a ferroptosis marker, 4HNE protein adduct formation decreased (Figure 5E,F). However, USP13 did not regulate the NFE2L2-SQSTM1 axis in the KRAS wild-type cell lines, H1299 and HBE. IKE causes upregulated of 4HNE as well (Figure 5G,H). These results suggest that in the case of KRAS mutations, the induction of ferroptosis in cancer cells would promotes autophagy and suppresses ferroptosis, and that USP13 might play an important role in the switch between the two types of RCDs.
Using the CRISPR-Cas9 splicing technique, we constructed the KRAS-knockout cell lines A549, H460, HBE, and H1299 (Fig. S6G and H). When KRAS was knocked out, the knockdown of USP13 significantly reduced cell viability in A549 and H460 cells (Figure 5I,J), whereas the cell viability of HBE and H1299 was not reduced compared with that of sgCtrl groups (Figure 5K,L). This indicated that in the case of KRAS mutation, USP13 knockdown promoted tumor cell death. We overexpressed KRAS WT or KRASG12S in the KRAS knockout cell line A549. Western blot results showed that KRASG12S was much more upregulated the USP13-NFE2L2-SQSTM1 axis and its downstream effector genes (KEAP1, SLC7A11, SQSTM1, LC3) than KRAS WT (Fig. S6I). The USP13-NFE2L2-SQSTM1 pathway was slightly activated when the cells were transfected with the KRAS wild-type construct, whereas the USP13-NFE2L2-SQSTM1 pathway was significantly activated when transfected with the KRAS mutant construct. We also overexpressed KRASG12S in A549 cells or treated the cells with the KRAS pathway inhibitor LY3214996 to activate or inhibit the KRAS signaling pathway. The results showed that the USP13-NFE2L2 axis was significantly activated upon KRAS pathway activation, the conversion of LC3B-I to LC3B-II significantly decreased, and 4HNE protein adduct formation increased in USP13-depleted A549 cells compared to the sgCtrl group, indicating autophagy switched to ferroptosis in USP13-depleted A549 cells (Figure 5M). However, the regulatory effect of the USP13-NFE2L2 axis was weakened by inhibitor treatment. When the KRAS pathway was inhibited, 4HNE protein adduct formation increased and the conversion of LC3B-I to LC3B-II significantly decreased in both the sgCtrl and sgUSP13 groups, further suggesting an antagonistic relationship between these two RCDs (Figure 5N). These results suggested that the USP13-NFE2L2 axis may be primarily used to facilitate ferroptosis in the autophagy switch to promote tumor progression, which is dependent on the activation of the KRAS signaling pathway.
NFE2L2 is a central player in depleted USP13 switching autophagy to ferroptosis
As USP13 increases the stability of NFE2L2, activates its downstream genes, and switches ferroptosis-to-autophagy, we hypothesized that NFE2L2 might be the key molecule causing these reactions. Under the TEM, the knockdown of USP13 was observed to result in a decrease in ALs and an increase in shrunken mitochondria compared to the sgCtrl at NFE2L2 WT status, whereas at NFE2L2 KO status, both the sgUSP13 and sgCtrl groups showed a significant increase in shrunken mitochondria (Figure 6A–C). Moreover, western blot showed that compared to the sgCtrl group, decreased USP13 expression reduced the expression of NFE2L2, SQSTM1, and SLC7A11 and the conversion of LC3B-I to LC3B-II. However, the regulation of sgCtrl and sgUSP13 on the expression of the above proteins disappeared with the NFE2L2 KO status (Figure 6D).
Based on the study of NFE2L2 participated in USP13 promoted ferroptosis-to-autophagy switch in vitro, we established a lung cancer cell xenograft mouse model. As shown in Figure 6E and Fig. S7A and B, compared to the sgCtrl group, the sgUSP13 groups showed suppressed tumor growth in NFE2L2 WT tissues, though not in NFE2L2 KO tissues. Similar results were additionally observed by western blot analysis of tumor tissues from nude mice (Figure 6F). TEM and morphometric analyses revealed decreased ALs and increased shrunken mitochondrial tumor tissue in the USP13 depleted group, though not in the sgCtrl group with NFE2L2 WT, whereas with NFE2L2 KO, both sgCtrl and sgUSP13 groups showed a significant increase in shrunken mitochondria (Figure 6G–I). Immunohistochemistry (IHC) analysis showed that the expression of NFE2L2, SQSTM1, SLC7A11, and LC3B, except for ACSL4, was significantly decreased in the sgUSP13 group compared to the sgCtrl with NFE2L2 WT, whereas SQSTM1, SLC7A11, and LC3B, except for ACSL4, decreased in the NFE2L2 KO along both the sgCtrl and sgUSP13 groups (Figure 6J). In the absence of NFE2L2, the depleted USP13 mediated switch from autophagy-to-ferroptosis was not obvious, implying that NFE2L2 plays a crucial role in the process of depleted USP13 promoting autophagy-to- ferroptosis switch.
Therapeutic targeting of the USP13 inhibits KRAS mutant LUAD growth by promoting ferroptosis
Spautin-1 is a specific and potent inhibitor of autophagy that suppresses the stability of USP10 and USP13 [40]. Therefore, we used spautin-1 to inhibit the expression of USP13 and observed its effects on the NFE2L2 signaling pathway. Treatment of A549 cells with spautin-1 led to a time-dependent reduction in the levels of USP13, NFE2L2, SQSTM1, and SLC7A11, and the conversion of LC3B-I to LC3B-II, except for ACSL4 (Figure 7A). We established a mouse model of lung cancer cell xenograft. When tumors reached a volume of approximately 100–150 mm3, the mice were treated with spautin-1 20 mg/kg via daily intraperitoneal injection. Finally, spautin-1 blocked the USP3 promoted tumor volume and weight increase (Figure 7B–D, Fig. S8). Except that ACSL4 was not affected, the spautin-1 group of tumor tissues also blocked the effect of USP13 reduction on the decreased NFE2L2, SQSTM1, and SLC7A11 protein levels and reduced the conversion of LC3B-I to LC3B-II compared to the DMSO group (Figure 7E). Hematoxylin-eosin (HE) staining showed that spautin-1 treatment increased the number of lipid droplets in the tumor tissue and antagonized the effect of the sgCtrl on decreasing lipid droplets in the DMSO group (Figure 7F). TEM and morphometric analyses revealed decreased ALs and increased shrunken mitochondrial tumor tissue in the USP13-depleted group, whereas after spautin-1 treatment, both the sgCtrl and depleted USP13 groups showed a significant increase in shrunken mitochondria (Figure 7G–I). Finally, IHC analysis showed that the expressions of NFE2L2, SQSTM1, SLC7A11, and lipidation of LC3B were significantly decreased, except for ACSL4, in the sgUSP13 group, whereas the expressions of USP13, SQSTM1, SLC7A11 and LC3B lipidation decreased, except for ACSL4, regardless of whether USP13 was knocked down after spautin-1 treatment (Figure 7J). These results indicated that intervention with USP13 expression might prevent tumor progression by inhibiting ferroptosis to the autophagy switch in KRAS-mutant LUAD, and that spautin-1 might promote autophagy to the ferroptosis switch.
Discussion
Autophagy is a conserved quality control process in evolution, that keeps cell homeostasis and inhibits tumorigenesis [2,58]. Paradoxically, autophagy is upregulated in cancers, sustaining their high metabolic rate and nutritional needs by freeing amino acids and other components from intracellular macromolecules degraded by lysosomes [59]. Dysregulation of the autophagy pathway also plays a context-dependent role in cancer, and interruptions to stimulate or prevent ferroptosis have been considered for cancer treatment or prevention [60]. Recent studies have shown that autophagy is positively associated with sensitivity to ferroptosis. Some upstream and downstream autophagy receptors, or danger signals are selectively required for ferroptosis-related autophagy [61]. However, the molecular mechanisms by which these two RCD modes regulate each other remains unclear.
USP13 participates in cancer development by regulating the stability of oncogenes or tumor suppressor proteins [40–42,62,63]. Among its functions relevant to tumorigenesis, USP13 mediates several RCDs. Similarly, N6-methyladenosine-modified USP13 enhances pro-survival autophagy and imatinib resistance by modulating the stability of autophagy associated protein 5 [43]. In addition, USP13 promotes apoptosis by promoting the stabilization of Mcl-1 in cervical cancer [64]. However, it remains unclear whether USP13 regulates RCDs other than autophagy and apoptosis. In this study, we found that USP13 activates NFE2L2 in three ways. First, USP13 decreased K63-linked ubiquitination of NFE2L2 (Figure 1L), increasing the stability of NFE2L2 for its activation. The structural domain of USP13 (aa 301–624) was important for the K63-linked ubiquitination of NFE2L2 (Figure 1O,P), implying that K63-linked ubiquitination is an important event associated with NFE2L2 stability and activation. Second, USP13 increased the proximity of NFE2L2 to SQSTM1 and reduced the interaction between NFE2L2 and KEAP1, releasing NFE2L2 from the inhibitory complex (Figure 2I–K, Fig. S5E and F). Third, USP13 enhanced the interaction between KEAP1 and SQSTM1, and enhanced the autophagic degradation of KEAP1 (Fig, 2K and L, Fig. S3C). Subsequently, using bioinformatics analysis, we found that USP13 May be involved in the regulation of ferroptosis rather than apoptosis and autophagy (Figure 4A). When tumor cells are under oxidative stress, the USP13-NRF axis is activated to inhibit ferroptosis, resist the damage caused by oxidative stress to tumor cells, and promote autophagy to provide more energy sources for tumor cells. Collectively, we showed that USP13 is a pro-survival protein that takes advantages of its components (autophagy, NFE2L2-SQSTM1; ferroptosis, and NFE2L2-SLC7A11) to keep tumor cells alive.
Generally, a decrease in SQSTM1 is associated with the activation of autophagy, and we were concerned about the increase in SQSTM1 protein levels when USP13 was knock down [43]. However, changes in SQSTM1 levels can be cell-type-and context-specific. For example, a decrease in SQSTM1 is associated with the blockage of autophagy because of its cleavage of the protein, along with other autophagy proteins, by calpains or caspases [65]. More importantly, activation of a signaling pathways such as RAF1/Raf-MAP2K/MEK-MAPK/ERK can also upregulate SQSTM1 and LC3 II protein levels and increase autophagy [66]. KRAS controls various of cellular behaviors by activating the core kinase cascade RAF-MAP2K-MAPK/ERK [67].
Here, the USP13-NFE2L2-SQSTM1 pathway requires the activation of the KRAS signaling pathway (Figure 5M,N, Fig. S6I), which further confirms the need for the KRAS signaling pathway to activate SQSTM1 and autophagy. In addition, an increase in NFE2L2 expression upregulates SQSTM1 and ubiquitin pathway proteins, thus promoting autophagy [56]. Therefore, the upregulation of SQSTM1 May be regulated by the KRAS pathway on the one hand and by the positive feedback of NFE2L2 on the other, and the co-upregulation of SQSTM1 and LC32 here means an increase in autophagy flux.
KRAS is the one of most common carcinogenic drivers in LUAD, and KRAS mutations occur in 32% of LUADs cases [68,69]. Compared to conventional chemotherapy, molecular targeted therapy significantly improves the survival rate of patients with targeted targeted lesions. However, no therapeutic molecules targeting KRAS-mutant LUAD have been clinically approved. KRAS-driven LUAD relies heavily on NFE2L2 to maintain mitotic signal activation [20]. USP13 is amplified in many types of human cancers, especially lung squamous cell cancers [41]. By analyzing 58 human NSCLC tissues, we found that high USP13 expression and NFE2L2 activation were strongly correlated in 30 of 39 KRAS-mutant LUAD cases (Figure 1D), further indicating gene amplification of USP13 May also be present in LUAD and relevant to the KRAS mutation. KRAS mutation often mediates metabolic reprogramming, highly active glucose metabolism, reprogramming of glutamine metabolism, and enhanced autophagy and micropinocytosis as well [68,70]. Aactivation of the KRAS signaling pathway, which activates NFE2L2 [20], may be an important signaling pathway for the USP13-NFE2L2 axis to regulate its downstream target genes (Figure 5M,N, Fig. S6I). A recent study found that mutant KRAS promotes USP13 expression through the transcription factor RREB1 [71], which means KRAS directly regulates USP13 at the transcriptional level and further validates our findings.
Furthermore, a major regulator that links autophagy and ferroptosis is NFE2L2. Autophagy and ferroptosis occur via the USP13-NFE2L2-SQSTM1/SLC7A11 axis and NFE2L2 KO strongly stimulate ferroptosis in vitro and in vivo (Figure 6), indicating that cancer cells without NFE2L2 May be incapable of switching from ferroptosis-to-autophagy.
Our experiments in vivo and vitro have confirmed that targeting USP13 promoted the switch from autophagy-to-ferroptosis and inhibited tumor growth in KRAS mutation LUAD cells and tissues (Figure 7). In addition to inhibiting autophagy and promoting apoptosis, spautin-1 promotes ferroptosis, and targeting USP13 could shifts autophagy-to-ferroptosis and inhibits tumor progression.
Moreover, this study revealed a crucial mechanistic coupling between the autophagy and ferroptosis programs in cancer cells. Depleted-USP13 mediated autophagy inhibition strongly stimulates ferroptosis, explaining why autophagy inhibition causes effective tumor starvation and regression, even when exogenous nutrients are abundant [25]. Furthermore, USP13 strongly blocks ferroptosis and activates autophagy, explaining why the inhibition of ferroptosis effectively promotes tumor progression. In this study, we identified USP13 as a regulator that take a comprehensively response to oxidative stresses and facilitates ferroptosis-to-autophagy (Figure 8).
Overall, this study highlights the significance of USP13 in the ferroptosis-to-autophagy switch and suggests that therapeutic modulation of USP13 could be a potential strategy to treat KRAS-mutant LUAD.
Materials and methods
Cell culture and stable lines
293T cells (American Type Culture Collection, CRL-3216) were cultured in DMEM (Gibco 12,491,015). HBE (CRL-2741), NCI-H1299 (CRL-5803), NCI-H23 (CRL-5800) and NCI-H358 (CRL-5807) cells, were obtained from the American Type Culture Collection and cultured in RPMI-1640 (Gibco 12,633,012). A549 cells (American Type Culture Collection, CRM-CCL-185) were grown in DMEM/F12 (Gibco 12,634,010). Culture mediums were added with 1% penicillin-streptomycin-gentamicin and 10% (vol:vol) bovine calf serum (Sigma-Aldrich, B7746). Cells were managed by mycoplasma clearance, and only mycoplasma-free cells were used.
Constructs
The construct expressing plvx-EEF1A1/EF1α-HA-USP13 with point mutation plvx-EEF1A1/EF1α-HA-USP13C345A was generated by standard molecular biology techniques for using Q5 ® Ultra-Fidelity 2X premix (New England Biolabs, M0492S) and QuickCut™ Dpn I (TAKARA BIO INC., 1609). Mammalian expression plasmids for pCMV-NFE2L2-GST-SV40-Neo (P37053), pCMV-KEAP1-3×MYC-Neo (G19630), pEnCMV-6×His-SQSTM1 (P20675), pLVX-EF1a-KRAS (human)-G12S-IRES-Puro (P31035), pLV3-U6-SQSTM1(human)-shRNA1-CopGFP-Puro (P47028), pLV3-U6-SQSTM1(human)-shRNA1-CopGFP-Puro (P46631), pLV3-U6-KEAP1(human)-shRNA1-CopGFP-Puro (P46708), and pLV3-U6-KEAP1(human)-shRNA1-CopGFP-Puro (P46824) were obtained from MiaoLingBio. USP13 mutants and truncations were kindly provided by Professor Bo Zhong (Wuhan University).
Antibodies and reagents
HRP-conjugated goat anti-mouse IgG (Cell Signaling Technology, 7076), HRP-conjugated goat anti-rabbit IgG (Cell Signaling Technology, 7054), anti-H3 (Cell Signaling Technology, 4499), anti-ubiquitin (Cell Signaling Technology, 3936), anti-LC3B (D11) (Cell Signaling Technology, 3868), anti-ACTB/β-actin (Sigma-Aldrich, F1804), anti-Flag (Sigma-Aldrich, F5441), anti-USP13 (Santa Cruz Biotechnology, sc -390,316), anti-TUBB/β-tubulin (Santa Cruz Biotechnology, sc -166,729), anti-KEAP1(Santa Cruz Biotechnology, sc -365,626), anti-GPX4 (Santa Cruz Biotechnology, sc -166,570), anti-His-Tag (66005–1), anti-MYC-Tag (16286–1), anti-HA (51064–2), anti-SQSTM1/p62 (18420–1), anti-NFE2L2 (16396–1-AP), anti-SLC7A11/xCT (26864–1-AP), anti-p-MAPK1/ERK2-MAPK3/ERK1 (28733–1-AP), anti-FTL/ferritin light chain polyclonal antibody (10727–1-AP) were purchased from Proteintech Group, Inc., anti-4HNE (abcam, ab46545), LY3214996 (MedChemExpress, HY-101494), Lys05 (Selleck, S8369), rapamycin (Selleck, S1039), cycloheximide (Selleck, S7418), chloroquine diphosphate salt (Sigma-Aldrich, C6628), MG132 (Sigma-Aldrich, M7449).
The CRISPR-Cas9-mediated USP13 knockdown (KD) and NFE2L2, KRAS knockout (KO)
293T cells were transfected of lentiCRISPRv2 plasmid (Addgene 52,961; deposited by Feng Zhang) which cloned into the single guide RNA with LipoMAX (Sudgen 32,012). Cells were selected with puromycin (1–2 μg/ml) for three days after transfection. Transfection efficiency was finally verified by real-time PCR. Guide RNA sequences targeting the USP13 gene are 5′- ACGCGGATCGTGGGCATGTG-3′, 5′-CACATGCCCACGATCCGCGT-3′; Guide RNA sequences targeting the NFE2L2 gene are 5′- TAGTTGTAACTGAGCGAAAA-3′, 5′-TTTTCGCTCAGTTACAACTA-3′; Guide RNA sequences targeting the KRAS gene are 5′- TCTCGACACAGCAGGTCAAG-3′. Single colonies with NFE2L2 or KRAS were selected and used for experiments.
Immunofluorescence analysis
Cells were washed, and harvested by trypsinization, and resuspended in 500 μL fresh PBS (Thermo Fisher Scientific, AM9625). 105 cells were cultured on a coverslip. The second day, cells were washed with PBS and incubated with culture medium containing 20 μM C11-BODIPY 581/591 (Thermo Fisher Scientific, D3861) in a cell culture incubator at 37°C for 30 min. After washing with PBS, cells were fixed in methanol for 10 min at −20°C, followed by blocking with 1% BSA (Beyotime Biotechnology, ST023) for 1 h at room temperature (RT). Then, cells were incubated with specific primary antibody overnight, followed by 1 h incubation with Alexa Fluor™ Plus 488 (Thermo Fisher Scientific, A21206) or Coralite Plus 650 (Proteintech Group, Inc, 3325), mounted ProLong™ Gold (Thermo Fisher Scientific, P36934), air-dried, and visualized, using a Biotek microscope.
Cycloheximide chase assay
Cycloheximide chase experiments were proceeded to confirm the protein stability, where cells were treated with cycloheximide (100 μg/ml) and the stability of the indicated proteins measured at indicated time point by western blot analysis.
RNA isolation and quantitative real-time PCR (qRT PCR)
Total RNA was extracted and purified by using Trizol reagent (Invitrogen 12,183,555). One μg of RNA was used for reverse transcription by using DNA reverse transcription kit (TAKARA BIO INC., RR037A), and qRT – PCR was performed using TB Green Advantage qPCR premixes (TAKARA BIO INC., 639676) according to the manufacturer’s protocols.
Immunoprecipitation assay
Cells were lysed in IP lysis buffer supplemented with protease inhibitor cocktails (Sigma-Aldrich, 20–116) for 30 min at 4°C and centrifuged at 13,000 g for 15 min. The supernatant was incubated with specific antibody and Protein G Dynabeads (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 10004D) at 4°C overnight. The Protein G beads were washed with ice-cold PBS three times, and the proteins were eluted from beads by boiling 5 min and proceeded for western blot analysis.
Deubiquitination assays
Cells were lysed in lysis buffer and the cell lysates were denatured at 100°C for 10 min in the supplement with 1% SDS. A portion of cell lysates (5%) were saved for immunoblot analysis. The rest of cell lysates (95%) were diluted with lysis buffer for denature-IP with specific antibodies. The immunoprecipitates were washed three times and subject to immunoblot analysis. In vitro deubiquitination assays, IP was performed to obtain ubiquitin-modified NFE2L2 from 293T cells cotransfected with GST-tagged NFE2L2 and His-Ubiquitin. The Flag-tagged USP13 or USP13C345A were eluted by the Flag peptide (Sigma-Aldrich, FlagIPT1). USP13 or USP13C345A protein was obtained by an anti-Flag affinity column in lysis buffer which contains 50 mm Tris-HCl, pH 7.8, 137 mm NaCl, 10 mm NaF, 1 mm EDTA, 1% Triton X-100 (Beyotime Biotechnology, P0096), 0.2% sarcosyl (Sigma-Aldrich 61,747), 1 mm DTT, 10% glycerol, and proteinase inhibitors. Ubiquitinated GST-NFE2L2 protein isolated by GST antibody and incubated with or without Flag-LSH in deubiquitination buffer (50 mm Tris-HCl, pH 8.0, 50 mm NaCl, 1 mm EDTA, 10 m MDTT, 5% glycerol) for 2 h at 37°C [40,72].
Transmission electron microscopy
A549 lung cancer cells and xenograft tissue were fixed and then observed by the Laboratory of Electron Microscopy, Pathology Department, Xiangya Hospital.
Mouse xenograft assay
The 5-wk-old female nude mice in this study were purchased from Hunan SJA Laboratory Animal Co., Ltd (BALB/c nude Mice). Then, 2 × 106 sgCtrl or sgUSP13 cells with NFE2L2 WT and NFE2L2 KO were injected subcutaneously into nude mice without matrigel. Tumor size was tested every 2 d with a caliper, and volume of mice tumor was calculated with the formula: L×W2 ×0.5, and L represents the longest diameter, W means the shortest diameter. 2 × 106 sgCtrl or sgUSP13 cells were injected subcutaneously into nude mice without matrigel. When tumors reached 100 to 150 mm3, mice were treated with spautin-1 (Selleck, S7888; 20 mg/kg) in 5% DMSO, 40% PEG300 (Selleck, S6704), 5% Tween80 (Selleck, S6702), and 50% water by daily intraperitoneal injection. Tumors were measured three times every week. Mice were sacrificed and cancer tumors were collected finally.
Histology and immunohistochemistry
Xenograft tissue samples were get and fixed in 10% formalin at 4°C overnight. Samples were submitted to the Department of Pathology, Xiangya Hospital for paraffin embedding, HE, and IHC staining. The antibodies used for IHC were USP13, NFE2L2, SQSTM1, KEAP1 (Santa Cruz Biotechnology, sc -365,626), LC3B, SLC7A11/xCT (abcam, ab307601), ACSL4 (Santa Cruz Biotechnology, sc -365,230).
Ethics approval
Lung cancer tissues were acquired from patients who were diagnosed with lung cancer between 2018 and 2021 at the Third Affiliated Hospital of Kunming Medical University (Kunming, Yunnan, China). All patients received a standardized surgery (length or width or height). The study was approved by the Institutional Ethics Committee of Kunming Medical University (Kmmu20230739). Informed consent for cancer tissue analysis was received before surgery. All animal experiments in this article were approved by Central South University, China (2021-XMSB-0066).
Statistical analyses
All the experiments were performed at least three times except the nude mouse experiments. Data of the experiments are analyzed as the mean ± SD or SEM. GraphPad Prism 9.0 software was used statistical analyses. Student’s t-test was used to decide the significant differences between two groups. Variance (ANOVA) was accessed to compare more groups. Differences judged statistically significant in the case as p < 0.05 (*p < 0.05, **p < 0.01, ***p < 0.001, ****p < 0.0001).
